analogy.p: Diffusion is like a ball rolling down a hill: it goes by itself and needs no energy. Active transport is like carrying the ball up the hill: it needs effort (energy from respiration), and you can carry it all the way to the top (a high concentration). A worker with a trolley (the carrier protein) takes one ball at a time up the slope. The analogy breaks down because in a cell the energy is used to change the shape of a protein, not to lift a weight against gravity.
analogy.t: Pushing a ball up a hill

bullets: **Direction**: from low concentration to high concentration (the opposite of diffusion).
**Energy**: supplied by **respiration** (made in the **mitochondria**).
It happens across a **cell membrane**, using special **carrier proteins** in the membrane.
Substances moved include **mineral ions** (e.g. nitrate, magnesium) and **sugar molecules** such as glucose.
Because it works against the gradient, it can build up a high concentration of a substance inside a cell, or take in a substance that is very scarce outside.
If respiration stops (for example no oxygen), active transport stops.
core.p: **Active transport** moves substances from a **more dilute solution to a more concentrated solution** (i.e. **against a concentration gradient**). This **requires energy from respiration**. The word "active" tells you the cell is doing work: it is an energy-requiring process, unlike diffusion and osmosis, which are passive. In an exam, a full-mark definition always includes both ideas: movement **against the concentration gradient** and use of **energy from respiration**.

bullets: Without active transport, a root hair cell could not absorb mineral ions once the soil concentration was lower than the concentration inside the cell.
Without active transport, glucose would stop being absorbed once the concentration in the gut equalled the concentration in the blood, so some glucose would be wasted in the faeces.
Active transport lets cells maintain different concentrations from their surroundings, which is needed for many processes.
The cost is **energy from respiration**, so cells that carry out a lot of active transport contain many **mitochondria**.
It is a **selective** process: only specific substances with matching carrier proteins can be moved.
Link to other topics: respiration (4.4) provides the energy; diffusion and osmosis (4.1.3) are the passive alternatives.
core.p: Diffusion can only move substances down a concentration gradient, so it can only equalise concentrations. Cells sometimes need to take in substances that are at a very low concentration outside (such as mineral ions in soil water) or need to absorb every last molecule of something valuable (such as glucose from the gut). When the concentration outside is lower than inside, diffusion would move the substance in the wrong direction, so the cell must use energy to move it in. Active transport is therefore essential to growth and survival.

bullets: **Step 1**: the particle (e.g. a mineral ion) attaches to a specific carrier protein in the membrane.
**Step 2**: energy from respiration is used and the carrier protein changes shape.
**Step 3**: the particle is released into the cell, on the side with the **higher concentration**.
**Step 4**: the carrier returns to its original shape and can pick up another particle.
Each carrier is **specific** to one type of particle, so the membrane controls which substances enter.
Carrier proteins are an extension to the specification wording, but they are the standard way to explain the mechanism in answers.
core.h: How active transport works: carrier proteins
core.p: The cell membrane contains **carrier proteins** that each recognise one type of particle. The particle binds to the carrier on the side with the low concentration. Energy released by respiration is then used to change the shape of the carrier protein so that the particle is released on the other side of the membrane, where the concentration is higher. The carrier then returns to its original shape ready to pick up another particle. The energy is what allows the movement against the concentration gradient.

bullets: **Soil water**: very dilute solution of mineral ions.
**Root hair cell sap**: more concentrated than the soil water.
Ions move **from the dilute soil solution to the more concentrated cell** by active transport, using energy from respiration.
**Nitrate ions** are used to make amino acids and then proteins for growth; a lack causes stunted growth and yellow leaves.
**Magnesium ions** are needed to make chlorophyll; a lack causes yellow leaves (chlorosis).
Root hair cells have **many mitochondria** to release the energy needed, and a **large surface area** (the hair) so more carrier proteins are in contact with the soil water.
Ions that have been absorbed move on into the xylem of the root and are carried to the rest of the plant.
core.h: Example 1: mineral ions into root hair cells
core.p: The concentration of mineral ions in the soil water is usually very low, and lower than the concentration inside the root hair cells. Diffusion would therefore move ions out of the root, not in. Root hair cells use active transport to absorb ions against the gradient. The plant needs these ions for healthy growth, so a plant that cannot absorb them shows deficiency symptoms.

bullets: The blood has a **higher glucose concentration** than the contents of the gut once most has been absorbed.
Active transport moves glucose **from the lower concentration in the gut into the blood (higher concentration)**.
It needs **energy from respiration**, supplied by the many mitochondria in the cells lining the small intestine.
This allows **all the glucose** to be absorbed, not just the amount that diffusion can move.
Glucose is **used for cell respiration**, which releases energy for the body.
The lining of the small intestine is adapted by villi (large surface area) so more carriers are available.
Link to other topics: digestion and absorption (4.2 Organisation), and respiration (4.4).
core.h: Example 2: glucose from the gut into the blood
core.p: After a meal, the concentration of glucose in the small intestine is often higher than in the blood, so glucose can move into the blood by diffusion. As digestion continues, the glucose concentration in the gut falls below that in the blood. Active transport is then used to move glucose against the gradient into the blood, so that as much as possible is absorbed. The glucose is carried round the body and used by cells for respiration.

bullets: **Diffusion**: net movement of particles from a higher to a lower concentration; passive; no energy from respiration needed.
**Osmosis**: net movement of water from a dilute to a concentrated solution through a partially permeable membrane; passive.
**Active transport**: movement of substances from a more dilute to a more concentrated solution (against a concentration gradient); needs **energy from respiration**.
Diffusion and osmosis **stop** (no net movement) when concentrations are equal; active transport can continue and create a concentration difference.

Rate of diffusion depends on concentration gradient, temperature and surface area; rate of active transport depends on **respiration** (oxygen, glucose, temperature) and the number of **carrier proteins**.
Active transport is stopped by **respiration inhibitors** (such as cyanide) or lack of oxygen, but diffusion is not.
core.h: Active transport compared with diffusion and osmosis
core.p: Examiners often ask you to describe differences, so you should have a clear comparison. Diffusion and osmosis are **passive**; active transport is **active**. Diffusion and osmosis move substances **down** a gradient; active transport moves them **against** it. Active transport requires carrier proteins and respiration.

bullets: **Oxygen concentration**: more oxygen allows more aerobic respiration, so more energy and a faster rate. Without oxygen the rate falls sharply.
**Glucose supply**: respiration needs glucose; a lack of glucose reduces energy and rate.
**Temperature**: warmer temperatures speed up the reactions of respiration and the movement of carriers up to a limit; at high temperatures proteins (enzymes and carriers) are **denatured**.
**Number of carrier proteins**: more carriers mean a faster rate; when all are in use the graph reaches a **plateau**.
**Respiration inhibitors** (e.g. cyanide) stop respiration and so stop active transport.
**Concentration gradient** matters much less than for diffusion because the cell uses energy to overcome it.
core.h: Factors affecting the rate of active transport
core.p: Because active transport relies on energy from respiration, anything that affects respiration affects it. This idea is used in data questions where a factor (oxygen, temperature, a poison) is changed and the uptake of ions is measured. Note that the rate does not simply keep rising: it levels off when all carriers are in use.

bullets: **Large surface area** of membrane (folded membranes or hairs) to hold more carrier proteins.
**Many carrier proteins** in the cell membrane.
Root hair cell: long hair shape increases surface area in contact with soil water.
Cells of the small intestine lining: folded surfaces (villi) and many mitochondria.
Always link the feature to its function: "many mitochondria, so more energy is released by respiration for active transport".
core.h: Adaptations of cells that carry out active transport
core.p: Cells that carry out a lot of active transport show features that help it work faster. These adaptations are a typical application question. **Many mitochondria** to release more energy from aerobic respiration.

bullets: If the substance is taken in when the **outside concentration is lower** than the inside, it must be active transport.
If uptake **decreases when oxygen is removed** or when a respiration poison is added, it needs energy from respiration, so it is active transport.
If uptake increases then **levels off** as oxygen increases, the plateau is because the **carrier proteins** are all in use (or another factor is limiting).
Compare concentrations by dividing: e.g. 0.04 ÷ 0.002 = 20, so the cell is **20 times** more concentrated than the soil water.
Quote data: "uptake of nitrate fell from 12 to 3 units when oxygen was removed".
If the concentration inside is lower than outside, diffusion alone could explain the movement, so you cannot be certain it is active transport.
core.p: Questions give data on uptake of ions under different conditions. To decide whether the uptake is by active transport or by diffusion, look at whether the substance is moving against the gradient and whether the process depends on oxygen or respiration. These data skills are often worth 3 to 4 marks.

bullets: State the concentration relationship: "the concentration of ions is lower in the soil than in the root hair cell".
Name the process: "active transport, against the concentration gradient".
State the requirement: "needs energy from respiration".
Link to structure: "the root hair cell has many mitochondria".
State the benefit: "so the plant gets the mineral ions it needs for growth".
core.h: A model way to describe and explain
core.p: For longer questions, the structure below picks up marks. Name the process, state the direction and the gradient, say what is needed (energy from respiration) and link it to the structure of the cell. Name the substance and where it moves from and to (e.g. mineral ions from the soil into the root hair cell).

bullets: **Digestion and absorption (4.2)**: absorption of glucose into the blood.
**Transport in plants (4.2)**: after uptake, ions move in the xylem; water follows by osmosis because the root cells have a lower water concentration.
**Cell structure (4.1.1)**: mitochondria and the cell membrane are the key structures.
**Homeostasis (4.5)**: substances such as glucose are kept at controlled levels in the blood.
core.p: Active transport links to many areas, which helps with synoptic questions. **Respiration (4.4)**: aerobic respiration in mitochondria releases the energy; glucose and oxygen are needed. **Photosynthesis and plant nutrition**: magnesium for chlorophyll and nitrate for protein, absorbed by active transport.

exam: **Define active transport (2 marks)**: "movement of substances from a **more dilute** solution to a **more concentrated** solution (**against** a concentration gradient) which needs **energy from respiration**".
**State/name (1 mark)**: e.g. "active transport", "mitochondria". Keep it short.
**Why active transport (2-3 marks)**: concentration lower outside than inside, so diffusion cannot move the substance in; energy is needed to move it against the gradient.
**Why root hair cells have many mitochondria (2 marks)**: mitochondria carry out respiration, which releases energy needed for active transport of mineral ions.
**Compare diffusion and active transport (3-4 marks)**: use comparative words: "whereas", "but"; give direction, energy, and carrier proteins.
**Why does uptake decrease without oxygen (2-3 marks)**: less aerobic respiration, so less energy released, so active transport slows.
**Graph questions (2-3 marks)**: describe the trend with data; explain the plateau as carrier proteins all in use or another limiting factor.
**Why are mineral ions needed (1-2 marks)**: nitrate for amino acids/proteins; magnesium for chlorophyll; link to growth.
**Calculation (2 marks)**: concentration ratio by dividing; show working and units.
**6-mark questions**: describe the process of active transport using the key words, an example (root hair or gut), the adaptation (mitochondria, surface area) and a comparison with diffusion.
**Common command word "Explain"**: always give a reason with "because" or "so".

mistakes.r: Active transport moves substances from **low to high** concentration (**against** the gradient) using **energy from respiration**.
mistakes.w: Active transport is the movement of substances from high to low concentration using energy.

mistakes.r: Write that it needs **energy from respiration**, which is the specification wording.
mistakes.w: Active transport needs ATP only, not respiration.

mistakes.r: Water moves by **osmosis**. Active transport moves **mineral ions** and **glucose**.
mistakes.w: Active transport is used to absorb water.

mistakes.r: The soil concentration is lower than in the cell, so ions are taken in by **active transport** against the gradient.
mistakes.w: Root hair cells use diffusion to take in mineral ions from the soil.

mistakes.r: Mitochondria **release energy** from respiration (energy is transferred, not made).
Without oxygen, aerobic respiration slows, so less energy is available and the rate of active transport falls.
mistakes.w: Active transport happens when there is no oxygen.

mistakes.r: The rate levels off (plateau) when the carrier proteins are all in use or another factor limits it.
mistakes.w: Active transport speeds up forever as oxygen increases.

mistakes.r: Glucose can diffuse when the gut concentration is higher, but when it is **lower** than in the blood, **active transport** is needed.
mistakes.w: Glucose is absorbed by diffusion only.

summary: AQA 4.1.3.3 asks you to know that **active transport** moves substances from a more dilute solution to a more concentrated solution (against a concentration gradient) and that this **requires energy from respiration**. You must know the two named examples: mineral ions into plant root hairs from very dilute soil solutions, and sugar (glucose) from the gut into the blood. You must also be able to compare it with diffusion and osmosis, which is a frequent exam question.

terms.d: The movement of substances from a more dilute solution to a more concentrated solution (against a concentration gradient), which requires energy from respiration.
The difference in concentration between two regions.
From a region of lower concentration to a region of higher concentration.
The chemical reaction in cells that transfers energy from glucose; it takes place in the mitochondria (aerobic).
Sub-cellular structures where aerobic respiration takes place, releasing energy.
A protein in the cell membrane that binds to a specific particle and moves it across the membrane.
The spreading out of the particles of any substance in solution, or particles of a gas, resulting in a net movement from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration.
The diffusion of water from a dilute solution to a concentrated solution through a partially permeable membrane.
A process that does not need energy from respiration.
Charged particles such as nitrate and magnesium that plants absorb from the soil for healthy growth.
A specialised plant cell with a long hair-like extension that gives a large surface area for absorbing water and mineral ions from the soil.
Mineral ions needed by plants to make amino acids and proteins.
Mineral ions needed by plants to make chlorophyll.
The part of a graph where the line levels off because another factor is limiting.
The part of the gut where digested food molecules, including glucose, are absorbed into the blood.

worked.ans: (a) 20 times more concentrated. (b) Active transport: nitrate ions move against the concentration gradient from the dilute soil water into the more concentrated cell, using energy from respiration.
worked.q: The concentration of nitrate ions in soil water is 0.002 mol/dm³ and in a root hair cell is 0.04 mol/dm³. (a) How many times more concentrated is the cell? (b) Name the process by which nitrate enters the cell and explain why. (4 marks)
steps: (b) The concentration in the cell is higher than in the soil, so nitrate moves from a lower to a higher concentration
Diffusion would move nitrate out of the cell, so energy from respiration is needed

worked.ans: (a) 75% decrease. (b) Less aerobic respiration means less energy released, so ions are taken up more slowly by active transport (the remaining uptake may be by diffusion).
worked.q: Roots in oxygenated water take up ions at 12 units. When oxygen is removed the uptake falls to 3 units. (a) Calculate the percentage decrease. (b) Explain the result. (4 marks)
steps: (b) Without oxygen there is less aerobic respiration
Less energy is released, so less active transport

worked.ans: Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a higher to a lower concentration and does not need energy from respiration. Active transport moves substances from a lower to a higher concentration (against the gradient), needs energy from respiration and uses carrier proteins, so it can continue after the concentrations are equal.
worked.q: Compare diffusion and active transport. (4 marks)
steps: Direction: diffusion is down a concentration gradient, active transport is against it
Energy: diffusion is passive, whereas active transport needs energy from respiration
Carriers: active transport uses carrier proteins
Equilibrium: diffusion stops when concentrations are equal, but active transport can build a higher concentration
